chunks: Open-loop op-amp: the comparator. The question: How does an open-loop opamp behave? What type of circuit is it?
An op-amp with no feedback compares its two inputs and pushes the output hard to one rail or the other. If the plus input is higher, the output goes to the positive rail.
If the minus input is higher, it goes to the negative rail or ground. That is a comparator: it answers "which input is bigger?" with a one or a zero.
Think of a doorbell button with a spring. Press even slightly past the threshold and it clicks fully on. Release below it and it clicks fully off. There is almost no in-between.
An open-loop op-amp is like that. The trouble comes if you hold the button right at the click point: small shakes make it flutter.
The output is a rail-to-rail square wave. It flips to +12 volts when the sine goes above the 0. 3 volts reference and back to minus 12 volts when it falls below.
The duty cycle is not 50% because the reference isn't zero: the output is high for the fraction of the cycle where sine theta 0. 3 .
The sine is drawn at 1 volts peak, so it's tiny relative to the output; the transitions look instantaneous because the gain makes the linear window only ±120 µV wide.
Comparator: a circuit that outputs a high or low depending on which input is larger. Rail: the supply voltage at which the output stops.
Threshold: the voltage on one input that the other is compared against. Hysteresis: using two different thresholds, one for rising and one for falling.
Schmitt trigger: a comparator with hysteresis, made by feeding part of the output back to the plus input (positive feedback).
Say a 5 volts op-amp has 2. 5 volts on the minus input as the threshold, and a signal on the plus input. At 2. 6 volts the output slams to 5 volts. At 2.
4 volts it goes to 0 volts. If the signal hovers near 2. 5 volts with a little noise, the output chatters. Adding positive feedback gives hysteresis, so it switches cleanly.
"Open loop, the op-amp's gain of 10 to the 5 or more acts on the tiny difference between its inputs, so the output slams to a rail depending on which input is higher.
That makes it a comparator, a one-bit ADC. The linear region is only ~100 µV wide.
Noise near the threshold causes chatter, so you add positive feedback for hysteresis, a Schmitt trigger.
In practice, dedicated comparators are better than op-amps for this because of faster recovery and logic-compatible outputs."
